newsitem.title: INDIA: India rejects Germany plea over nuclear test pact.
newsitem.headline: India rejects Germany plea over nuclear test pact.

text.p: Germany on Friday said India's opposition to a global nuclear test ban was hurting its chances of becoming a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council, but India reiterated its unflinching opposition to the pact.
"We think India is entitled to claim a permanent seat and so India is a candidate whom we support," visiting German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told a news conference.
Kinkel said that in talks with Indian leaders he tried to point out the relationship India's bid to become a Security Council member and its controversial Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) stance.
"There is some connection," Kinkel said through an interpreter. "It would be wrong to deny that some connection does exist."
Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral, speaking at the same news conference, reiterated New Delhi's opposition to the CTBT, which has been signed by almost 140 nations.
"India will not sign the CTBT, either now or later," he said. "India is in favour of the abolition of nuclear weapons, but the CTBT is neither comprehensive nor would it ban tests."
The Security Council currently has five permanent members -- the United States, China, France, Britain and Russia.
Both Germany and India are pushing to become members. Nigeria's military ruler said on Thursday his country, as well as India and Brazil as regional powers, deserved to be members.
Trinidad and Tobago Prime Minister Basdeo Panday, another visitor to Delhi, also backed India's Security Council drive. "The time has come for India to have that honour," he said.
But Kinkel, who is Germany's second-highest official after Chancellor Helmut Kohl, said India's United Nations campaign has been hampered by its staunch opposition to the CTBT.
Kinkel noted that last year, after India rejected the CTBT, New Delhi fell far short in its bid to be elected to one of the rotating non-permanent Security Council seats.
Japan won 142 votes for the Asian non-permanent seat in last October's balloting compared with Australia's 91 and India's 40.

India, which stood in near isolation against the treaty while it was negotiated last year, claims it would allow the five declared nuclear powers, who are also Security Council permanent members, to continue laboratory tests.
New Delhi has insisted that the nuclear powers agree to commit to a timetable for nuclear disarmament.

A U.N. working group has been discussing enlarging and reforming the council for nearly three years. It is widely accepted that, if any new permanent seats are created, two of them should go to Germany and Japan.

But Gujral called for a significant widening of the Security Council. "Reforms must not be piecemeal, they must be wholesale," he said. "We do not agree that one, two, three should be admitted and the rest should wait."
India's campaign to join the Security Council has been part of a broader drive to play a greater role in regional and international security while opening its economy to the world.

Kinkel said Germany also backed India's drive to join the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) and to be included in a summit between Asia and European Union member states to be held later this year in London.
